passages.t: Sweet as honey, and seven days among the exiles
passages.happening:
God tells Ezekiel to eat the scroll and then speak to the house of Israel. ‘So I ate, and it was as sweet as honey in my mouth’ (verse 3). He is not being sent to foreigners of hard speech, who would have listened, but to his own people, who will not listen because they will not listen to God (verses 5-7). So God will make his forehead ‘like a diamond, harder than flint’ (verse 9).

The Spirit lifts him up, and he hears the great rumbling of the living creatures' wings and wheels (verses 12-13). He goes ‘in bitterness and in the anger of my spirit, with the strong hand of the LORD upon me’ (verse 14). He comes to the exiles at Tel-abib by the Kebar, ‘and for seven days I sat where they sat and remained there among them, overwhelmed’ (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
Eating the scroll was a vision, not a meal, but it drew on real pictures. Honey was the sweetest thing an Israelite knew, and the psalms call God's words sweeter than honey. The sweetness is the sweetness of receiving God's word, even when the message is lament.

A hard forehead was an idiom for stubbornness. God will make his prophet more stubborn than his hearers.

Tel-abib comes from a Babylonian phrase for a ruin mound, an old settlement destroyed long before. Deported peoples were often settled on such places to rebuild and farm them. Sitting for seven days echoes the customs of mourning, when friends sat with the grieving for seven days.
passages.later: The psalm says God's ordinances are ‘sweeter than honey’ (Psalm 19:10). Job's friends sat with him on the ground for seven days and seven nights (Job 2:13).
passages.asks: Before Ezekiel said anything, he sat where the exiles sat for seven days. Ask whom you need to sit with before you speak. And ask what it would mean to share someone's grief before you try to fix it.

passages.t: The watchman, and the silent prophet
passages.happening:
After seven days God says, ‘Son of man, I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel. Whenever you hear a word from My mouth, give them a warning from Me’ (verse 17). Four cases follow. If Ezekiel does not warn the wicked, they die in their sin and he is responsible. If he warns them and they do not turn, he has saved himself. The same is true for the righteous who turn to sin, or who heed the warning and live (verses 18-21).

Then God shows Ezekiel his glory again on the plain, and tells him to shut himself in his house. His tongue will stick to the roof of his mouth, and he will be silent, except when God opens his mouth to speak. ‘Whoever listens, let him listen; and whoever refuses, let him refuse’ (verse 27).
passages.hearers:
The watchman was a familiar figure. He stood on the wall or a tower and warned the town when an enemy approached. If he saw danger and kept quiet, the blood of those who died was on his head. God gives that task to the prophet.

The four cases are written like case law, the same style as chapters 18 and 33. Ezekiel's silence seems to mean that he would speak only when God gave him a word, and not as an ordinary public speaker. His mouth is opened fully when news of Jerusalem's fall arrives (33:22).
passages.later: David's watchman stood on the roof of the gate and called out what he saw (2 Samuel 18:24-27). In Jezreel a watchman on the tower saw Jehu's troops coming and reported it to the king (2 Kings 9:17).
passages.hard:
Does verse 20 mean that God puts stumbling blocks before righteous people, and that they can lose all their righteousness?

On the stumbling block, many interpreters understand it as the occasion of judgment God brings on someone who has already chosen evil, not a trap set for an innocent person; Ezekiel uses the phrase elsewhere for what leads to ruin (7:19; 14:3). On losing righteousness, the passage is about personal responsibility: past good deeds do not buy immunity for present rebellion, and past wickedness does not doom someone who turns. It is not a full teaching on whether believers can finally fall away. Christians who hold that true believers cannot fall away read it as a warning that exposes false righteousness, or as speaking of judgment in this life. Christians who hold that believers can fall away read it as a real warning to them. Both agree that it calls for perseverance, and that God takes the choice between life and death seriously.
passages.asks: The watchman's task was to warn, not to force. Ask whether there is someone you have a responsibility to warn, gently and honestly. And ask whether you are listening to the warnings God has given you.
